content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a parallelized version of PSRO, called Efficient PSRO (EPSRO).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, while I think the paper has some merits I find it lacking in two important areas: novelty when considering existing literature (in particular Anytime PSRO/AODO), and choices regarding the experimental evaluation.

1. Comparison to AODO. It seems to me that ESPRO is exactly the same algorithm as AODO, with two small changes:
- The addition of warm starting
- The inclusion of elements from Pipeline PSRO
However, from the ablation results it seems that warm starting doesn’t improve over not warm starting, unless combined with parallelism. Also, parallelism alone seems to have a negligible effect too. This synergy is surprising and I am having a really hard time trying to understand how the two elements would interact in a way where one without the other wouldn't work, but the combination would produce a large effect. In other words, why is it reasonable to expect that warm-starting and parallelism be synergistic? I found the paper lacking in that respect. 

2. One of the main benefits of PSRO-type methods is their scalability. Yet, unless I missed something, it seems that the games the methods are tested on are tiny. Kuhn poker has 12 actions across all infostates of any player, and Leduc poker less than 1000 if I recall correctly. These games can be solved in milliseconds by the simplex algorithm. The same goes for random matrix games, or the AlphaStar matrix game. Am I missing something important here? Why are the authors testing a method whose main feature is scalability on tiny toy games? Perhaps this is standard for technical reasons within the PSRO literature and I am simply unaware of it, but I would have appreciated a remark on this discrepancy. 

3. To my understanding, Theorem 3.3 just says that as I go forward one iteration (and expand the restricted set), I do better against the opponent *from last iteration*. However, it is not immediately obvious to me that this is equivalent to showing that the exploitability decreases as you expand the restricted set and solve the URR game, which would seem like the more meaningful "potential function" to decrease monotonically. Did I miss anything?

4. Multi-agent gathering seems to not be a two-player zero-sum game, so it seems to be outside of the scope of the rest of the paper. If my understanding is correct, what was the point of the experiment, and how is the algorithm implemented (specifically regarding the fact that the agents have non-zero-sum payoffs) and why? What guarantees can be recovered?

---

Nits and typos:
- StraCraft -> StarCraft
- The capitalization in several bibliographic entries is incorrect (e.g., words like Cambridge, PSRO, Starcraft).
- Multi-agent gathering is sometimes spelt with capital letters and sometimes without
content.summary_of_the_review: I find the experimental evaluation of the paper lacking, with important aspects left unexplained

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies considers an algorithmic approach based on the policy space response oracle (PSRO) method for finding approximate Nash equilibria in Markov games. The proposed approach aims to improve two aspects of PSRO, referred to in the paper as computational and exploration efficiency. The approach is called efficient PSRO (EPSRO) and is based on solving unrestricted-restricted meta-games using no-regret learning algorithms. The authors provide convergence results of their approach and evaluate it against baselines on several different environments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
The novel algorithms appears to empirically outperform baselines algorithms on several different domains, increasing the rate of convergence to a Nash equilibrium, and reducing the compute time. To achieve these results, the proposed method combines several different principles from prior work to achieve these results, most notably no-regret learning is baked into the algorithmic approach and appears to be a sensible way to find approximate Nash equilibria of unrestricted-restricted meta-games. The paper also aims to provide theoretical guarantees of the proposed method.   
---
**Weaknesses** Despite these strengths, in my opinion, the paper has quite a few weaknesses:
- First, the paper is not written very well. I generally found the details behind the introduced techniques hard to grasp, and to some extent, I'm still quite confused about the main contributions of this work. For example, it's not entirely clear to me what is the key insight that this paper introduces that is different from the techniques studies in the literature. The paper seems to combine several different ideas from prior work, including those introduced in (Zinkevich et al., 2007) and (McAleer et al. 2020) --- in my opinion, the current description does not adequately disentangle the contributions of this paper from prior work. It also doesn't help that the concurrent work, McAleer et al. 2022,  builds on the approach of Zinkevich et al., but was not used as one of the baselines in the experiments. 
- The formal setting and the theoretical analysis are not entirely clear. Based on the abstract, one may conclude that the focus is on zero-sum games, but the formal setting does not clearly specify this. Moreover, one of the games, multi-agent gathering, appears to be a general sum game.. However, if the settings considers  general-sum games, then I don't fully understand the theoretical results. No-regret learning in general-sum games converges to a set of course correlated equilibria, while the paper focuses on approximate Nash equilibria. It would be quite helpful to have an adequate literature review of the recent results from the learning in games literature, explaining how they relate to the results of this paper.  
- Following up on my previous point, it is not clear to me what one should conclude from the results from Section 3.2, since they are primarily about Algorithm 3, not the full EPSRO algorithm (although theorems 3.8 and 3.9 use EPSRO in their titles...). It's also not clear to me why some of these results hold. E.g., the proof of Theorem 3.9 applies in its first step Theorem 3.8 on both $\pi_i$ and $\sigma_{-i}$, however Theorem 3.8 only holds for $\sigma_{-i}$, which has a restricted set of strategies. In contrast, $\pi_i$ is chosen from an unrestricted set. Given this, shouldn't step 2 of Algorithm 3 apply a no-regret learning algorithm designed for adversarial MDPs? It would be useful to clarify these technical details. 
- There are also some details that seem to be missing in the experimental results. For example, NEPSRO is used but not explained, ablation studies are only reported for one domain, some of the results (e.g., in Fig 5) don't report confidence intervals, etc. Additionally, the plots are really hard to read, in part, because the font is too small.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Please also see my comments above. I summarize my main points regarding quality, clarity, and originality below. 
- Clarity: As I already mentioned, I found parts related to theoretical results hard to follow. I also believe that the paper does not adequately convey the key ideas of this work and how they differ from prior work. The main part of the paper is not self-contained. For example, step 3 of Algorithm 3 references Algorithm 5 in the appendix, while the text does not provide intuition behind step 3 of Algorithm 3. Some of the claims are misleading. For example, the abstract says: *Theoretically, we prove that the proposed optimization procedures of EPSRO guarantee the monotonic improvement on the exploitability, which is absent in existing researches of PSRO*. On the other hand, the paper  references the work of McAleer et al. 2022, which reports similar results on exploitability.  
- Quality: The paper reports results which indicate that the proposed approach improves performance relative to the baselines. So, overall, the approach seems promising, but it is also hard to properly evaluate the reported results as the clarity of the paper could be considerably improved. I haven't checked all the details, but overall, the results reported in the experiments look reproducible.
- Originality: The paper has a lot of overlap with the existing works on PSRO. Most notable are references (Zinkevich et al., 2017), (McAleer et al. 2020), and (McAleer et al. 2022), with the latter one being a concurrent work. The authors do discuss differences between their approach and these works, however, the key conceptual ideas of this work look quite similar those reported by prior work.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the experimental results indicate the the proposed algorithmic approach leads to improved performance, and hence, looks promising. However, the presentation of this work could be considerably improved, and at the moment, I'm not fully confident that the results, as currently presented, are complete nor entirely correct.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies Nash equilibrium finding in two-player zero-sum games. The central contribution is an algorithm called Efficient PSRO (EPSRO), which is designed to improve PSRO in terms of efficiency, i.e. the number of simulations required to find equilibrium. Some theoretical guarantees are established for EPSRO, while superior empirical performance is demonstrated on matrix games and extensive-form games.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
1. The algorithmic techniques developed in this work, including practical ways of using warm-starts and parallelization, are novel and could be interesting to the multi-agent RL community.

**Weaknesses:**
1. The paper, especially the algorithm, is not presented in an organized manner and is hard to understand. See more on clarity below.
2. The main algorithmic idea, namely relaxing the restricted-restricted metagame in PSRO to an unrestricted-restricted game, seems to nullify one benefit of using PSRO namely efficiency when the Nash equilibrium has very small support.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I should start by emphasizing that I am not very familiar with the line of work based on PSRO and its advantages, and it is likely that I misunderstood parts of this paper.

**1. Why not just run no-regret learning on the matrix game?**

It is well-known that in two-player zero-sum matrix games, playing no-regret leads to Nash equilibria. Examples of no-regret algorithms include Hedge/MWU, FPTL (Follow-the-perturbed-leader), etc. What are the benefits for using a seemingly complicated and roundabout approach, which includes MWU as a subroutine, instead of just directly running a no-regret algorithm?

One reason for preferring PSRO is that the Nash equilibrium could have small support and thus be found with smaller computational cost by PSRO.  However, this advantage is undermined by the EPSRO, which again considers the full action set (for one player). Another reason might be that EPSRO is best-response based; however, FPTL is also best-response based (see e.g. Suggala et al.).

**2. How exactly does the algorithm performs its updates?**

In Algorithm 3, the key update (line 3) is performed with Algorithm 5, which further points to Lemma B.7 for the update of $\beta$, which still doesn't state clearly the update rule of the algorithm. This, compounded by the typos and sloppy writing, leaves the reader completely at lost about what the algorithm does. For example, judging by the proof of Theorem 3.8, the algorithm is supposed to use some equivalent form of MWU since the proof of the regret bound directly evokes the regret bound of MWU. However there seems to be no justification at all that line 7 in Algorithm 5 performs MWU. The only argument presented is Lemma B.4, which is a tautology and bears no apparent relation to the algorithm per se. Is the solution to Eq. (13) the same as Eq. (8)? I don't believe that is true, and even it is, it is not mentioned at all.

**3. The overall writing is sloppy and almost obscure.**

Examples of sloppy writing: In Eq. (13), $x$ is $k-1$ dimensional while $\bar{\sigma}_{-i}'$ seems to be $k$ dimensional, how do they even subtract? The first term in Eq. (13) seems to be a scalar. Why should one take the 2-norm of a scalar, instead of just the absolute value? What does "initial" mean? Is there any relation at all between the statement of Lemma B.7 and its proof?

==========

Suggala et al. Follow the perturbed leader: Optimism and fast parallel algorithms for smooth minimax games
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a new algorithm for a well-studied problem, namely solving two-player zero-sum matrix games. Despite the development of some interesting techniques and empirical evidence in favor of the algorithm, the overall obscurity of the presentation prevents the reader from understanding how even the algorithm updates, and why should one choose the new algorithm over classic methods.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WEse: WE CANNOT AGREE WITH YOUR REVIEW
content.comment:
After reading the review, I believe the Reviewer WEse indeed misunderstood our contribution, also the problem we researched. PSRO aims to solve large-scale/complex two-player games/tasks, which have a long horizon to simulate, or large infosets to explore, instead of trivial matrix games. The matrix games introduced in our paper are just for rapid validation and comparison with other PSRO methods. That's one of the reasons why we didn't compare it with no-regret learning. If you really read the paper carefully, you should know even the solving of matrix games also follows learning-based rules in our settings. Moreover, I want to emphasize that EPSRO aims to improve the efficiency of using small support to solve large-scale/complex tasks instead of what you conclude in your review.

**How exactly does the algorithm perform its updates?**

> The algorithm performs updates by following Algorithm 5 for meta-strategies and classical reinforcement learning for best-responses. B.7 aims to figure out the initialization of meta-strategy $\beta$, i.e., the warm-starting; Line 7 in Algorithm 5 is a deterministic update, i.e., we update only the logit that relates to the maximum of return, which is different from its original stochastic update in MWU; (13) is the initialization of $\beta$, not a solution to (8), please read it carefully.

**The overall writing is sloppy and almost obscure.**

> Please note $$(x-\bar{\sigma}_{-i})^{\top}\bar{l}^e_{-i}$$ is a scalar, also $\bar{\sigma}'_{-i}(k)u_{-i}(\bar{\pi}_i,\pi^{e+1}_{-i})$, so there is no problem to do minus between them; It is a straightforward idea to optimize the distance between two scalars with 2-norm, absolute value maybe also fine; "initial" means initialization.

**The main algorithmic idea, namely relaxing the restricted-restricted metagame in PSRO to an unrestricted-restricted game, seems to nullify one benefit of using PSRO namely efficiency when the Nash equilibrium has very small support.**

> We think the reviewer misunderstood the computation of best responses in PSRO. Please read the definition of the URR game carefully. In EPSRO, the unrestricted part only serves to compute best-response, while the restricted part serves to learn meta-strategies.
>
> For any PSRO method, they search for a best-response from an unrestricted policy set at each epoch. As for the learning of meta-strategies in EPSRO, it is still derived from a restricted policy set. Thus, I cannot agree with you that such a setting will "nullify one benefit PSRO". In contrast, such a setting will make a best-response achieves a lower exploitability, i.e., closer to an approximate  Nash.
>
> And the main differences between traditional PSRO and EPSRO include 1) the production of opponent meta-strategies and 2) how to support the best response computation. In PSRO, the opponent's meta-strategies are computed by solving a restricted-restricted game, then the computed meta-strategy will be used to learn best-response. However, such a setting has a drawback in that the computed best-response prefers to overfit to the fixed opponent meta-strategy, and performs smaller gamescape and higher exploitability. We have explained all of them in our original submission, you can read them in the section introduction, Theorem and etc.
